_meta: Ten points scattered around a straight-line relationship, used to show that the confidence interval for the fitted line and the prediction interval for a new observation are different intervals answering different questions, and that using the narrow one to say where a new data point will fall badly understates the spread. A fitted regression line has two kinds of uncertainty around it. The confidence interval (confidence band) captures uncertainty in the line itself -- how well the data pins down the average response at a given x -- and it shrinks toward zero as the sample grows, because more data locates the mean ever more precisely. The prediction interval captures where a single new observation will land, which is the line's uncertainty PLUS the irreducible scatter of individual points around the line; it therefore adds the residual variance and never shrinks below roughly one residual standard deviation no matter how much data you collect. The two are often confused because both are drawn as bands around the same line, but the confidence band can be far narrower than the scatter of the actual points -- narrower than the noise itself -- so it contains only a small fraction of individual observations, while the prediction band is built to contain about 95% of them. Reporting a confidence band as 'where the next point will be' is the error. x and y are the observations; k is the multiplier for an approximate 95% interval (2 standard errors). The fitted line, the residual standard deviation, the confidence and prediction half-widths, and the fraction of the points each band contains are computed. Stdlib only.
